title: The world inches toward catastrophic climate events: 'Bigger shocks are on the way'
description: The devastation causes the world's nations to unite to combat climate change.  Scientists have long warned that the world will experience more intense extreme weather events like heat waves, storms, f...
fullText:
NEW YORK (AP) — In the opening scene of American writer Kim Stanley Robinson's "The Ministry for the Future," a heat wave combined with a breakdown of the electrical grid in India kills 20 million people. The devastation causes the world's nations to unite to combat climate change.

Scientists have long warned that the world will experience more intense extreme weather events like heat waves, storms, floods and droughts. But what once seemed like the realm of fiction is now discussed as a possibility, even an inevitability.

Warning about an "extreme of extremes" or the "Other Big One," a play off the California reference of a big future earthquake, can be fraught. After all, nobody can say for sure when a weather catastrophe may happen. But in the last few years, the planetary ingredients needed for a massive disturbance have been building. And alarm is growing.

"The risk is that people just think you are exaggerating," said Daniel Swain, a climate scientist with the California Institute for Water Resources. "It's the 'Boy Who Cried Wolf' problem. Sometimes wolves are real. If it's outside the door, wouldn't you want to know?"

In the 1850s, while living in Seneca Falls, New York, amateur scientist Eunice Newton Foote did a series of experiments that put different substances, including carbon dioxide and moist air, inside glass cylinders and left them in the sun. What she found was extraordinary: cylinders with carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas that is released when coal, gas or oil is burned, heated up faster and took longer to cool after the sun went down.

Fast-forward: Today, Earth is being heated by massive amounts of greenhouse gases being pumped into the atmosphere, leading to a gradual rise in average global temperature. That increase, 1.44 degrees Celsius (2.59 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer in 2025 compared to the early 1800s, leads to more frequent, and more intense, extreme weather events.

The country that has released the most greenhouse gas, and thus contributed most to climate change, is the United States. But don't expect recognition of that, much less major government-led efforts to combat it, as the country marks its 250th birthday. President Donald Trump has called climate change "the greatest con job ever," referred to climate policies as a "Green New Scam" and said U.N. climate predictions were made by "stupid people."

At any given time there are numerous extreme weather events happening around the globe. Indeed, some have already been so big that we have arguably entered an age of extremes.

Consider Australia's "Black Summer" of wildfires in 2019 and 2020, when 19 million hectares (over 46 million acres) were scorched. Or Pakistan in 2022, when flooding left a third of the country under water. Or Hurricanes Milton and Helene in 2024, which ravaged parts of the southern United States. That is to say nothing of periodic smaller disasters, such as last year's Texas floods that engulfed young campers; the Los Angeles wildfires that chewed through entire neighborhoods; and Typhoon Kalmaegi, which walloped Vietnam and the Philippines.

Sarah Perkins-Kirkpatrick, a climate scientist at Australian National University, says she had a "come to Jesus moment" when she realized that constant extreme weather events wouldn't stop even if the world could immediately reach net zero, the point when as much greenhouse gas is taken out of the atmosphere as released into it. Many countries and major companies have net-zero targets for 2050 or beyond.

Because carbon dioxide can remain in the atmosphere for hundreds of years, and so much has already built up, the damage could take centuries to reverse. And we keep adding more.

"It's the issue of the frog in the boiling water," said Perkins-Kirkpatrick. "If we get used to bracing ourselves, are we going to notice?"

What's clear is that no country is truly prepared for a major climate disaster, and the risks are changing.

Robinson, whose book was published in 2020, says if he were writing today he would include a chapter on wildfires, which have become larger and more destructive. And while the potential heat disaster he writes about in India would arguably be less likely today, thanks to less reliance on the grid and use of solar power, Robinson believes the risks of catastrophe have increased.

The book, he says, "still has a purpose."

It's basic psychology to avoid talking about uncomfortable things. Climate change, depressing and overwhelming, falls into that category.

Instead of taking action by radically reducing greenhouse gas emissions, or updating our infrastructure to live in a world altered by extreme weather events, a common response, from governments to individuals has largely been to ignore it. Part of the challenge is the care scientists must take when discussing extreme events.

It's impossible to say, for example, that a disaster will happen in a certain year or even decade. But modeling improves every year, and the amount of time between extreme events is shrinking.

Sonia Seneviratne is a Swiss climatologist who vice chairs a working group of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, the top U.N. body of climate scientists. Seneviratne likens the risk to smoking and lung cancer. People who smoke won't necessarily get lung cancer, but the chances are higher and doctors should say that. Similarly, the risk of massive extreme events rises with every tenth of a degree.

"If such an event happened, I could already see the criticism of people saying, 'Climate scientists didn't tell us,'" Seneviratne said. "But we did."

While earthquakes are not connected to climate change, the way many cities in earthquake-prone California have prepared for a potential Big One is as an example of what's possible. Central to that effort has been Lucy Jones, a seismologist and author of "The Big Ones: How Natural Disasters Have Shaped Us (and What We Can Do About Them)."

In 2014, Jones, then with the U.S. Geological Survey, worked with Los Angeles Mayor Eric Garcetti's administration in developing an initiative that produced widespread retrofitting and earthquake preparedness in LA, and then later in other California cities. Two years later, she formed a nonprofit that advises on preparing for earthquakes and other disasters.

Jones says people will make changes if they believe risks are real and solutions are possible. Without that belief, the response will likely be to ignore the issue.

"Climate denial is one way of coping," said Jones. She said people rationalize by thinking, 'I won't believe it's true, so I'll feel safer.'"

Over the last quarter century, many movies have focused on extreme weather events, which provide action and danger to any plot. The cinematic portrayals usually have one of two endings: everything will be okay or we are doomed.

Consider two popular climate movies that came out 15 years apart. In the 2004 "The Day After Tomorrow," Jack Hall, played by Dennis Quaid, is a climate scientist who, speaking at a U.N. climate conference in Delhi, urges a major reduction in greenhouse gas emissions, warning that a failure to do so will lead to major extreme weather events.

"The climate is fragile," says Hall.

"The economy is fragile," responds the U.S. vice president.

Shortly after, the disaster that Hall warns about happens. Melting polar ice halts the North Atlantic Current, which moves warm ocean currents northeast across the Atlantic. There are giant cyclones, massive hailstones, heavy flooding and tornadoes before a big freeze takes over — so cold that anybody outside dies.

Eventually the vice president, who has become president, apologizes to the nation for exploiting nature.

In the 2021 satire "Don't Look Up," two astronomers played by Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence discover a giant comet heading toward Earth. They try to spur action to avoid annihilation. The U.S. president, played by Meryl Streep, isn't interested.

"At this exact moment, I think we sit tight and assess," Streep says after learning the comet is heading straight toward Earth.

"How big is this thing? Can it destroy my ex-wife's house?" jokes a television news host.

At the end, almost everybody dies, a scenario that even the worst predictions of climate impacts don't envision.

As powerful as extreme weather events have already gotten, much worse is likely to come. It's basic physics.

More than half all greenhouse gases produced by humans throughout history have been released into the atmosphere over 50 years. Those gases create heat, which scrambles weather patterns and ecosystems.

The when of a major climatic event, or more likely several in different parts of the world, can't be known with certainty. A catastrophic event in any given area could be in 50 years, or 10 years, or sooner.

People who deny climate change is real will point out that scientists get projections wrong, and it's true that not every climate model has been correct. But over the last decades, if anything, climate scientists have been too conservative. Climate impacts are happening much faster than predicted.

One of many examples: in January 2022, the U.K. Climate Risk Assessment said there was a 0.02% chance of 40C (104F) or above heat before 2040. That summer, parts of the U.K. topped 40C.

We have also reached a moment when "tipping points" — when deterioration of a given planetary system has crossed a threshold from which it can't recover — are no longer positioned as theoretical or futuristic.

The most commonly cited is corals. According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, between 2023 and 2025, 84% of the world's corals suffered the expelling of microscopic algae in response to heat stress, which often leads to dying. Even if temperatures were to sharply drop, the recovery of most corals is doubtful.

The Amazon rainforest, which stores massive amounts of carbon dioxide and helps regulate the climate, is also at risk of a tipping point. Persistent drought, large wildfires and deforestation to make way for cattle have degraded swaths of forest in recent decades. The debate today is when, not if, the Amazon will release more carbon dioxide than it holds.

This year's El Niño, a natural and periodic warming cycle, is expected to be the strongest ever recorded, which could push temperatures even higher, breaking records and leaving damage along the way.

Overall, the Earth is on a dangerous path.

"We need to be talking about some of the worst things that can happen," said Tim Lenton, climate science professor at the University of Exeter. "It's natural to think that some bigger shocks are on the way."

title: Seven uncapped players in Ireland's WXV squad
description: Ireland head coach Scott Bemand says it is "particularly pleasing" to name seven uncapped players who impressed in the Women's Interprovincial Championship in his squad for the WXV Global Series.
fullText:
Ireland head coach Scott Bemand says it is "particularly pleasing" to name seven uncapped players who impressed in the Women's Interprovincial Championship in his squad for the WXV Global Series.

Forwards Jemima Adams Verling, Sophie Barrett, Beth Buttimer and Kate Jordan will all be hoping for a Test debut next month, as will backs Caitriona Finn, Lucia Linn and Alana McInerney.

Ireland will play USA and Japan at home in September, before a pair of October Tests against South Africa in the new format of WXV.

In between, they will also play a second game against Japan that does not form part of the series.

Munster trio Buttimer, Finn and McInerney were involved in the wider Six Nations squad this year, as were Connacht's Adams Verling and Ulster prop Barrett.

Second row Jordan and centre Linn, however, have been called up for the first time.

Munster have led the way in the Interprovinvial Championship with three wins from three and will play Leinster in the final of the competition on Saturday.

Connacht wing Beibhinn Parsons is also included despite missing the western province's first three games through injury.

"It's particularly pleasing to see seven uncapped players included," said Bemand.

"The Interpros highlighted the quality of talent coming through the system, and this is an excellent chance for those players to challenge themselves, bring their own strengths to the group and help raise standards as they push for international honours."

As well as those who have been fighting it out in the colours of their provinces this month, Bemand has also called on eight players based in England.

Gloucester Hartpury trio Neve Jones, Niamh O'Dowd and Sam Monaghan are all included, as are Brittany Hogan of Sale Sharks and Trailfinders' back-three player Niamh Gallagher.

Exeter's Cliodhna Moloney-MacDonald and Dorothy Wall are also among the 36-player panel but there is no place in the squad for their Chiefs team-mate Nancy McGillivray.

title: Former world snooker champion Dott guilty of child sex abuse
description: The former world champion was found guilty of lewd and libidinous behaviour towards a girl and boy.
fullText:
Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been found guilty of child sexual abuse.

The 49-year-old denied two charges of lewd and libidinous behaviour towards a girl and a boy between 1993 and 2010.

During a trial, the High Court in Glasgow heard that Dott had exposed himself and inappropriately touched a primary school girl in the 1990s and attacked a young boy between 2006 and 2010.

Lord Harrower told Dott, who won the World Snooker Championship in 2006, he would be sentenced at a separate hearing in Edinburgh on 29 September.

Dott covered his face with his hands and shook his head while the verdict was delivered by jurors following a five-day trial.

He previously called the allegations made against him "disgusting".

Lewd and libidinous practices refer to any sexual crimes against children committed prior to 1 December 2010.

The offence was abolished in 2009, but is still used for crimes carried out before then.

During the trial, the court heard how Dott had "caressed" the girl's bottom while giving her a piggyback and that, on another occasion, he had exposed himself to her.

On another occasion, she said Dott suggested she "take her trousers down" and lifted her top and began kissing her stomach after asking if she wanted to "play a guessing game".

The girl, now a woman in her 40s, said Dott would kiss her, touch her inappropriately and carried out a sexual act that would, if committed now, amount to rape.

She said she recalled the "smell" of creams Dott used for a skin condition after he kissed her and that the actions left her "shocked and scared".

The court heard how Dott bought her a teddy bear with a love heart on it in the course of the abuse.

Police previously contacted Dott about the allegations in 2001, but no charges were brought.

The woman gave a new statement to police in 2025.

During his evidence, the boy said his abuse at the hands of Dott began not long after he defeated Peter Ebdon to win his sole world title at The Crucible in Sheffield in 2006.

The boy, now a man in his 20s, said he was about eight years old when Dott molested him in a shower at a home in South Lanarkshire.

He told the court how Dott "rewarded" him with crisps and fizzy drinks and once handed him a £50 note, only to accuse the boy of stealing it when his parents found out he had the money.

He also said he was abused in a car on a number of occasions and "inappropriately touched" while Dott played online poker.

Dott had told the trial the allegations were false and that he had "never acted inappropriately with anyone".

Det Insp Gary Smillie, of Police Scotland, described Dott as a "dangerous individual".

He added: "I hope this conviction provides some measure of comfort to those impacted by his crimes.

"His conviction is as a direct result of their strength in coming forward and providing information which assisted our inquiries."

Lord Harrower was told the woman had provided a victim impact statement for him to consider before sentencing next month.

Dott was taken into custody until then.

The World Professional Billiards and Snooker Association (WPBSA) said it had permanently revoked Dott's membership with immediate effect.

This followed an emergency board meeting board where it was unanimously agreed to removed him from the sport.

The WPBSA has also written to World Snooker Tour (WST) to request his immediate removal from the WST Hall of Fame.

Dott was previously suspended from all professional snooker activities on 9 April 2025 pending the outcome of his trial.

He was subsequently relegated from the professional ranking list at the conclusion of the 2025/26 season.

description: Harry Wilson made history at the City Ground by becoming the 900th player to represent Leeds United in a senior competitive fixture.The Wales international was named in Daniel Farke’s starting line-...
fullText:
Harry Wilson made history at the City Ground by becoming the 900th player to represent Leeds United in a senior competitive fixture.

The Wales international was named in Daniel Farke's starting line-up for the opening Premier League game of the 2026/27 campaign, helping the Whites secure a dramatic 1-0 victory over Nottingham Forest.

Wilson joined Leeds on a free transfer during the summer after leaving Fulham and made his competitive debut alongside fellow new arrivals Tarik Muharemović (898) and James Trafford (899).

The landmark appearance came as Leeds began the new season with all three points, secured by Anton Stach's superb late free-kick.

Wilson is the latest player to claim a landmark place in the club's history, following Pierre-Michel Lasogga, who became the 800th player to represent Leeds in 2017.

Before him, Alex McCarthy reached the 700 mark, Seb Carole was the 600th and former England international Mark Hateley became number 500.

The earlier milestones belonged to Ian Baird at 400, Jim Storrie at 300, Jimmy Rudd at 200 and James Wilson, who became the club's 100th senior player.

The latest Wilson to wear the white shirt has now completed the journey to 900, marking the occasion with a winning debut on the banks of the River Trent.

title: The future of a Manchester City midfielder is now painstakingly clear
description: If there was any further proof needed that Nico Gonzalez is surplus to requirements at Manchester City, it arrived yesterday. Marc Guehi started in midfield ahead of the Croatian international in City...
fullText:
If there was any further proof needed that Nico Gonzalez is surplus to requirements at Manchester City, it arrived yesterday. Marc Guehi started in midfield ahead of the Croatian international in City's 2-1 win over Bournemouth. It was also revealed before the match that City had finally reached an agreement with Lille to sign Ayyoub Bouaddi. While Nico Gonzalez is happy to remain at Manchester City and fight for his place, the club are willing to sell the Spanish midfielder. It has now been reported that Newcastle United are edging closer to signing Nico Gonzalez. That looms as the best move for Nico, whose card seems marked at City.

Fabrizio Romano reported last night that Newcastle United had made significant progress in their bid to sign Nico Gonzalez from Manchester City. Romano reports that the two clubs have almost agreed on a deal that will see the Spanish midfielder join Newcastle's rebuild. Furthermore, it is reported that Newcastle are in talks with Nico Gonzalez in a bid to seal the deal early this week.

Unfortunately, Nico Gonzalez has likely played his final game for Manchester City. He has spent 18 months at the club after signing for City from FC Porto in January 2025. During his time at the club, the Spanish midfielder showed signs that he could play an important role for the FA Cup and Carabao Cup holders. Nico could play as a defensive midfielder and he did step up in Rodri's absence last season. Looking at Enzo Maresca's current squad, it did seem like Nico Gonzalez could play that role this season.

But it isn't to be. For whatever reason, City have decided that it would be better to sell Nico Gonzalez. Perhaps the City hierarchy feel that the Spanish midfielder is a good midfielder, but not capable of reaching the level they desire. Perhaps Nico Gonzalez' isn't suited to playing in an Enzo Maresca side. Whatever their reasoning is, City seem poised to sell Nico to Newcastle.

Newcastle United are eager to sign Nico Gonzalez from Manchester City. After seeing Marc Guehi start ahead of fhe Spanish midfielder yesterday, a summer transfer may be exactly what Nico Gonzalez needs.

MOSCOW, Aug 24 (Reuters) - The Kremlin said on Monday that measures were being taken ‌to minimise the impact of Ukrainian strikes ‌on Russia's grain exports as global wheat importers brace for ​tighter supplies amid attacks on Black Sea grain infrastructure.

Tit-for-tat attacks by Russia and Ukraine, both major grain exporters, on ports and vessels in recent weeks ‌have shuttered grain ⁠terminals and forced shippers to delay or cancel loadings for dozens of cargoes ⁠during the peak export season.

"Measures have been identified and will be further developed, ensuring that all ​grain intended ​for export is shipped ​on time and in ‌full," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.

President Vladimir Putin acknowledged last week that Russia was experiencing problems with its agricultural exports, but said it would resolve them. The Kremlin chief also pledged ‌that there would be no ​shortages on global markets.

title: Scott's world title aim after testing personal period
description: Olympic champion Hannah Scott is preparing for the World Championships in Amsterdam which begin on Tuesday after her "most successful winter of training so far".
fullText:
Olympic champion Hannah Scott says she will arrive at the World Rowing Championships in Amsterdam on the back of her "most successful winter of training so far".

The Coleraine sculler says her experience to date in the sport is becoming "more and more useful, which is even showing across the team".

Scott won Olympic gold in Paris two years ago but her story has been a rollercoaster ride of injury and illness as well as success and joy.

On the water, life is good, and the public will get to see that this week as Scott and her team-mates compete in the Netherlands.

But, away from competition, elite athletes like Scott face the same challenges as anyone else and she has opened up about some of the issues she has had to navigate.

"In my personal life, I've had my hiccups and ups and downs. My life was turned upside down at Christmas time, when I went through a serious breakup and I've had to manage that," said Scott.

"But in terms of my life in the boat and training, I've managed to keep that all going this year and it shows in terms of my performances.

"That was the one thing I was really stubborn about. I wasn't going to let anything happening in my personal life impact my rowing and my career which I've put so much work towards."

Compartmentalising life and not bringing personal problems to training that could affect performance and other athletes around them is part and parcel of life as an athlete.

It is something Scott has learned to do, especially during that difficult spell last year which coincided with an important period of training.

"When I talk about what happened at Christmas time, it all happened during a really testing period in rowing. We were going through a lot of trials which ended up dictating a bit of our selection for the year," she added.

"I actually didn't share a lot of what was going on at Christmas time, because I knew everyone in the boat would probably then be worried about what was happening.

"You tell your friends, you get the support where you need it, but in terms of when you're in training, and for me, working in such a high-pressure environment, that type of thing can actually distract quite a lot.

"It's easier to try and find your support systems where you can with your family and your friends, and then keep your performance separate, because when you bring too much emotion into it, even happy emotion, I do think it can sometimes distract you from what you're trying to do.

"It's a skill I've had to learn a lot 

Scott is now setting her sights on winning a second world title in the women's quad sculls alongside fellow Northern Ireland rower Finnola Stratton as well as Imogen Grant and Lola Anderson.

In Amsterdam they will face world champions the Netherlands on home water, but Switzerland and Germany will also provide stiff opposition.

There is also a new quad from Ireland that includes 19-year-old Sophia Young from Belfast, who recently took silver in the single sculls at the world under-23 championships.

"The event itself is starting to stack up, and that's where I'm excited to see where we land on it, because, with everyone else that's improving, I think we've seen a massive breakthrough, is how I would describe it, in the past five weeks and what we've done in our crew," added Scott.

"I want to see where that lands and how that lands and hopefully we can display that in what's going to be an amazing event at this World Championships."

title: Four arrested over murder of two-time world champion Tete
description: One of the suspects is due in court on Monday to be charged with murder and attempted murder.
fullText:
Four people have been arrested in South Africa in connection with the murder of boxing champion Zolani Tete, who was shot dead outside his home on Friday.

Tete, 38, was gunned down in what has been described as an ambush in Mdantsane, Eastern Cape. A young woman who was with him was also shot and is in hospital.

One of the men being held, a 22-year-old who was arrested on Saturday, will make an initial appearance in court on Monday, and faces murder and attempted murder charges.

Tete held the WBO bantamweight title from 2017 to 2019, as well as the IBF super-flyweight title in 2014. He was later given a four-year ban, which lapsed in July this year.

The remaining suspects, who were arrested on Sunday, are due in court on Tuesday. Two have been charged with unlawful possession of firearms and ammunition. It is unclear whether they will also be charged with murder and attempted murder.

Tete was in his car waiting for the gate to his house to open when two armed suspects in balaclavas emerged from a vehicle and fired "multiple shots" at him and a 27‑year‑old female passenger, according to officials.

The motive behind the attack is unclear.

Tributes have been pouring in for the two-time world champion since his death. South Africa's Sports Minister Gayton McKenzie said: "South Africa has lost one of the finest fighters it has ever produced."

Former Sports Minister Fikile Mbalula also paid tribute to Tete, lamenting the loss of a "a great South African who has made an immense contribution in the sport of boxing".

Tete beat Liverpool's Paul Butler in 2015 in one of the eight times he fought in the United Kingdom.

He also holds a Guinness World Record for the fastest knockout in a title fight, ending his match with Siboniso Gonya inside 11 seconds in 2017.

Tete last fought in July 2022, beating Briton Jason Cunningham by knockout In London, but it was later ruled a no-contest after he failed a drugs test.

He tested positive for anabolic steroid stanozolol and was given a ban by the UK Anti-Doping Agency.

After his death, manager Mla Tengimfene confirmed he had been training for a comeback fight after his ban ended.

Tete had 29 wins in 34 fights, with four losses and one no-contest.

South Africa has one of the highest murder rates in the world.

According to the latest crime statistics, covering the period between January and March this year, around 58 people were killed each day.

title: Maradona's 'Hand of God' ball sells for £2.5m
description: The football with which Diego Maradona scored his famous 'hand of God' goal in the 1986 World Cup quarter-final victory over England is sold at auction.
fullText:
The football with which Diego Maradona scored his famous 'hand of God' goal at the 1986 World Cup has sold at auction for £2.5m.

Maradona famously punched the ball past goalkeeper Peter Shilton in Argentina's 2-1 quarter-final win over England.

After the game, he told reporters it had been scored "a little with the head of Maradona and a little with the hand of God".

Maradona later scored what became known as the 'goal of the century' in the same game, dribbling past five England outfield players before slotting the ball past Shilton.

Though it sold for $3.3m (£2.5m) at Heritage Auctions in the United States on Saturday, the ball had been expected to fetch nearer $10m (£7.3m).

Speaking to Reuters before the auction, Mike Provenzale, a specialist auctioneer at Heritage, said: "It's a true one-of-one item. Arguably the most significant soccer item that exists."

Tunisian Ali Bin Nasser, who refereed the match in 1986, collected the Adidas Azteca ball at full-time and kept it for more than three decades.

In 2023, he signed a letter to confirm it was the only ball used during the match, which has also been confirmed by further independent authentication.

Bin Nasser sold the ball in 2022 for $2.37m (£1.74m). Its new owner again put it up for auction in 2023 though it did not sell as bids did not meet the minimum value set.

The shirt worn by Maradona during the same match sold for £7.1m at auction in 2022.

Infantino must remember he is European - Ceferin
description: Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin says his Fifa counterpart Gianni Infantino's attempt to sell off a stake in the World Cup was "worse than the Super League".
fullText:
Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin says Gianni Infantino needs to remember he is European after describing his Fifa counterpart's plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup as "worse than the Super League".

Earlier this month the world governing body abandoned Infantino's proposal to create a new company - Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) - to manage the commercial and ticketing rights of all Fifa competitions, with 21% to be sold off to a private investment company.

Uefa led opposition to the plan, with its members voting to boycott World Cups unless it was scrapped.

European football's governing body has since said it has lost confidence in Infantino, while the football associations of all the home nations have withdrawn support for the 56-year-old Swiss.

"I think this plan is even worse than the Super League plan," Ceferin told the Rest is Politics podcast., external

"Super important clubs wanted to do their own league, which is wrong, and would destroy football. But in this case, football would be literally sold.

"I'm absolutely sure that the plan is dead. It's hard to to imagine what kind of people would sell the sport that belongs to everyone. We will not allow that to happen."

The European Super League was a proposed breakaway league of 20 top European clubs as a rival to Uefa's Champions League, but the project fell apart days after its unveiling in April 2021 after widespread criticism.

Ceferin said that Uefa had no prior knowledge of Infantino's plan, and that he found out through the media while on holiday with his family.

"He didn't contact me since this happened," Ceferin said.

"They [Fifa] play on, you know, '[how] arrogant Europe is against us: They have enough money, but I help the small and the poor'.

"But I think someone should remind him that he is a European, and that he was supported by Uefa, which he forgot."

Infantino - who worked at Uefa for 16 years, and was general secretary for nine - has been flying around the world in the search of public support.

On Saturday, he met with Caribbean Football Union members in the Dominican Republic and on Sunday he was at the E-Sports World Cup in Paris, attended by the French President Emmanuel Macron, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and Portugal forward Cristiano Ronaldo.

Infantino asked to stay away from youth tournament

Scottish FA withdraws support for Fifa president Infantino

Ceferin confirmed he would not run to become Fifa president at the Fifa Congress in March 2027, when Infantino will look to secure a fourth term in the role.

"I'm not interested because of two reasons. One reason is that I love Uefa and I love working here, and I think that at a certain point it's time also to enjoy life a bit," the 58-year-old Slovenian said.

"And the second point is, my credibility is much, much, much higher if I'm not interested in the position."

Before his aborted FFE proposal, Infantino was coming under increasing pressure over his relationship with United States President Donald Trump.

After US striker Folarin Balogun had a red card suspension overturned so that he could play in his side's defeat by Belgium in the last 16 of this summer's World Cup, Trump revealed he personally called Infantino to request the sanction be lifted.

Earlier this month, Trump said it would be a "terrible mistake" to remove Infantino as Fifa president.

"That was more than shocking. We have rules, and if you don't respect your own rules, then the game doesn't make any sense," Ceferin said on the incident.

"The president of a country says: 'I called him, and I told him to look at it.' And then the Fifa president says it was an independent decision.

"I mean, for us as football fans, or for us as a governing body, that's shocking. That's shocking, and - trust me - almost everybody was shocked. Just not everybody dared to speak."

title: China probes use of formaldehyde to keep cabbages fresh
description: Using the carcinogen to preserve food is prohibited in China, the world's largest producer of cabbages.
fullText:
Authorities in China have launched an investigation into reports of formaldehyde being used to preserve the freshness of cabbages for human consumption.

Officials in the northeastern Hebei province confirmed that they had verified footage showing individuals dipping cabbages in a solution before loading them onto trucks for transportation.

An environmental blogger first released the footage last week. Using formaldehyde, a colourless chemical that is known to cause cancer, for preserving the freshness of food in China is strictly prohibited.

China is the world's largest producer of cabbages, most of which are exported to neighbouring countries in Asia.

Police have taken legal action against the individuals involved, according to state media.

Officials are now moving swiftly to prevent panic and restore confidence by carrying out spot checks on markets across the country.

Chinese state media says investigators will also establish how widespread the practice is and take measures to trace affected vegetables.

In a statement issued on Saturday, local authorities in Kangbao county said: "Any illegal or non-compliant practices discovered will be dealt with strictly in accordance with the law to ensure the safety of the vegetable supply."

Xinfadi market in Beijing, one of the major sources of fresh produce in the capital, issued a statement saying that it had investigated the source of its cabbages, adding that none of the affected vegetables had entered its market.

The incident has generated widespread media attention in China.

An editorial in the People's Daily wrote: "The wholesalers focused solely on their immediate economic interests while completely disregarding the lives and health of consumers. [They] crossed a legal red line and breached the moral bottom line."

China produces well over 30 million tons of cabbages each year, nearly half of the world's annual total. Vietnam, South Korea and Russia are among the largest export destinations for the vegetable.

Exposure to relatively high quantities of formaldehyde in some workplaces has been linked to some types of cancer in humans, but the effect of exposure to small amounts is less clear, according to the American Cancer Society.

title: Using international football to reignite Premier League dreams
description: Before his potential Premier League debut for Fulham, BBC Sport looks at the role international football has played in the development of players like Shea Charles.
fullText:
On an August afternoon at Queen Ethelburga's College in York eight years ago, Michael O'Neill could never have known he was about to set eyes upon two players who would go on to become two of his most important Northern Ireland internationals.

It was then that Shea Charles, who has just become NI's most expensive-ever player at the age of 22, and Isaac Price both donned a Northern Ireland shirt for the first time against Leeds United's Under-16s in a friendly.

The duo played as part of a Club NI side - the academy for Northern Ireland at the time - alongside the likes of Liverpool's Conor Bradley and Portsmouth's Terry Devlin.

It was the first step along an international pathway that would see the pair win senior caps as teenagers under O'Neill before they had established themselves at their clubs. Both are now among the first names on the manager's teamsheet.

In the summer window, Charles became the most expensive Northern Ireland footballer when he joined Premier League side Fulham for £30m from Southampton, who he had joined after leaving Manchester City in 2023.

"You could see straight away there was a player there," said O'Neill as he recalled the first time he watched Charles in 2018.

"I suppose that's one of the biggest pleasures we've had with this team because we've known these boys from such a young age."

Charles' rise to NI's most expensive footballer

Dallas backs Charles to thrive at Fulham

As the examples of Charles and his younger brother, Pierce, show, eligibility is key for a nation with a playing pool as small as Northern Ireland.

Sometimes players are scouted, sometimes the parents or agents of players approach the Irish FA, or clubs can alert the association to eligible players.

Sometimes, however, it is a case of being in the right place at the right time.

Joe Shields, who was head of youth recruitment at Manchester City at the time, got to know the Charles family and knew the brothers would be eligible through their mother, Mary, who comes from Northern Ireland.

After watching Shea progress, Shields contacted Andy Cousins, who was also working at City with emerging talent and with the Irish FA, and recommended that it would be good for his development to get involved in the pathway with Northern Ireland.

From there, Cousins introduced O'Neill to the Charles and Price families ahead of their debuts for the Club NI side.

While O'Neill says he was "being polite and saying hello", it also served a bigger purpose. For an up and coming player like Charles, it left a lasting impression.

"It was really cool for us, to be able to see that the senior manager had that interest in the youth team," said midfielder Charles, who has won 35 caps since making his NI debut in March 2023.

"It was really good to see that he does look at those younger age groups and for boys who maybe have a chance to come through.

"It really helped me get to know the boys, the coaches, the whole set-up and eventually going on my first senior camp and making my debut. It was really special and shows that the pathway was really important."

O'Neill says it is important for him to see the next generation of talent long before they get on the fringes of the senior team, and that the work of Andy Waterworth, director of elite player development, and his staff gives him an opportunity to be in the thick of things.

"I think we're really good at that as a small association," he said.

"With the time frame at that age, it can go quite quickly so there's lads I'm seeing in our academy and I may well be the manager that gives that player his debut."

Cousins, who said Charles "didn't have a worry in the world" at City and "just loved playing football", believes that O'Neill's work with the players at a young age allows him to trust them at senior level, which may not happen at other associations.

"It's allowed him to believe in them and put them on the pitch young and early," said Cousins, who now works as head of scouting at Chelsea alongside Shields, who is co-sporting director at Stamford Bridge.

"I think he worries less about the physical elements, and if he thinks they're going to be a really good player long term, it's about getting them in quickly to try and be at that level."

O'Neill says there are two threads to developing Northern Ireland's playing pool, through domestic-based players and those recruited through eligibility.

There are the success stories of Charles and Price, who came through at Everton before establishing himself at senior level with Standard Liege and West Brom.

But O'Neill adds that if a club releases a player or if their future is uncertain, that the JD Academy - the successor to Club NI - offers stability to help them continue to develop as footballers.

O'Neill pointed to the stories of Dan Ballard and Pierce Charles, who were released by Arsenal and Manchester City respectively, but were still selected by Northern Ireland's youth teams to continue their development.

Now, Ballard is a key player for Sunderland - alongside fellow NI defender Trai Hume - and this summer Charles re-joined Manchester City from Sheffield Wednesday before going on loan to Queen's Park Rangers.

"Their futures were very much in the balance. Pierce was released from Man City at 16, but we don't release him from Northern Ireland.

"It's very important to keep the boys involved as much as we can and try and help and support them when those difficult situations arise."

Shea Charles said the story of his brother was "really important" and it was positive for his development to stay involved with Northern Ireland.

"When Pierce left City, he always had those [Northern Ireland underage] games to play in.

"He always had a spot in those teams and was still able to show what he can do at that high level. I feel that can be the same for so many lads."

O'Neill highlighted the example of Ethan Galbraith, who won his first cap as an 18-year-old in 2019 when he was at Manchester United but only broke into the NI team with more regularity when he was 23 and working his way back up the football ladder with Leyton Orient.

With that time and patience, he is now an integral part of O'Neill's squad and earned a move to Stoke City from Swansea in the summer window.

"You can see the potential in all the young players, but their careers never go in an upward straight line all the time," O'Neill added.

"We never write young players off. We understand that at times they may have difficult times at their clubs, but that's natural. It's a competitive environment."

Despite having smaller resource compared to larger nations, O'Neill believes the IFA's scouting team "doesn't miss very much" when it comes to eligibility.

"We're constantly working at it and we're having conversations with various lads who are at different stages of their careers as well.

"I wouldn't ask a young player to do an international transfer unless I thought they genuinely had a chance to come and be a senior international. I think that's very important."

The second strand is with domestic-based players within Northern Ireland.

Of O'Neill's current squad, players like Trai Hume, Conor Bradley, Ethan Galbraith and Ruairi McConville are all graduates from the pathway.

With the next generation, Ceadach O'Neill and Braiden Graham are examples of getting senior Northern Ireland experience while still featuring at underage level for Arsenal and Everton respectively.

Both players have been in the JD Academy and featured for Irish Premiership side Linfield before they made the move to England.

Charles says that while it is a different pathway than the English club system, the benefit of training and playing together has been beneficial for his team-mates.

"The boys talk about how it was really good for them," he said.

"I'm sure it was a bit different to England, but the end goal was always the same to get to the senior squad, so credit to them."

He adds the fact that, no matter where their football journey started, that they have all come through the underage ranks together has been beneficial at senior level.

"I feel like you can see it on the pitch, with the way we play, and how we talk to each other and congratulate each other.

"When we get a bad result, you can see the way we get around each other. It's a really great group."

Before Club NI was formed, there was a community programme but the full JD Academy, as it is now known, allows the most promising young footballers in Northern Ireland to participate in a residential programme at Campbell College, as well as the benefits that come with playing international football at a young age such as nutrition and strength and conditioning.

For O'Neill, it has been one of the "biggest pluses" since he took over as manager for the first time in 2012, saying the academy has done a "phenomenal job".

"I think we have something which a lot of associations are quite jealous of," he said.

"If you're in a big country, the clubs develop the players because they've got the resources to do it, but our clubs can't do that.

"Not every player in the academy is going to go and be a professional player or will play for Northern Ireland at senior international level, but it is giving them a really good opportunity at a critical time in their development path."

While the Championship is a strong league with consistently challenging opposition, playing international football has allowed Charles to play - and hold his own - against some of the best players of the world.

In the past three years, he has faced Rodri for Spain just before they won the European Championships, Germany's Florain Wirtz, Sandro Tonali for Italy and France's midfield pairing of Aurelien Tchouameni and Adrien Rabiot.

On each occasion Charles held his own - particularly against Italy, where he was arguably the best player on the pitch against Tonali and Nicolo Barella.

On Monday night, the 22-year-old could make his Fulham debut against Xabi Alonso's Chelsea, a potential second Premier League appearance coming three years after his debut under Pep Guardiola at City.

It could be a full circle moment for Charles, as he will be reunited with Cousins and Shields, who played a role in the development of the likes of current Chelsea midfielders Cole Palmer, Morgan Rogers and Romeo Lavia, who came through at City alongside Fulham's new recruit.

"It's much easier to benchmark players when you can say that you've played against players from the Premier League or certainly the top five leagues in Europe," said Cousins.

"Especially where the Premier League is so demanding physically, to see people performing well at that level, it's much easier to trust that and to be able to sign a player.

"I think Shea will be absolutely no problem at all, as he's shown in his performances against those big teams he has played against in the last two years."

Charles agrees and says facing the world's best players has helped him prepare for the Premier League.

"To be in that Premier League environment and hopefully to make my Fulham debut on Monday would just be incredible," Charles said.

"It'll be really cool playing the best players in the world every week.

"I look forward to playing with Northern Ireland and being able to experience those games, even if it's a friendly like the Spain or France games.

"It's does prepare you for what the best players are like, so I'm really looking forward to it."

title: Wales pushing the pain barrier in bid to improve
description: BBC Sport spends a day in Wales' pre-season camp, watching players put through their paces ahead of the new WXV Global Series.
fullText:
Sweat is pouring off Alisha Joyce and Georgia Evans as they emerge exhausted from the spin bike chamber at Wales' training base.

They collapse to the floor fighting for breath as head coach Sean Lynn gives them an encouraging tap on the back.

Next door in the gym Maisie Davies changes the playlist to "It's my birthday" while the forwards go about completing their sets in search of personal bests.

And out on the artificial pitch, Ashley Beck is putting the backs through their paces, with uncapped Amy Williams catching the eye.

This is just a glimpse of life in Wales' camp and for the players three weeks of pre-season pain is almost over.

But for Lynn and the other coaches the hard work continues as they must whittle down the squad for next month's WXV Global Series.

Neumann back in Wales' extended WXV training squad

New-look Wales end losing streak with Barbarians win

Wales kick-off their campaign against South Africa at Cardiff Arms Park on 18 September before hosting USA on 26 September. They will then head out to Japan for two further Tests on 23 and 31 October.

All three opponents are ranked above 12th-placed Wales, who have lost their last nine competitive fixtures.

And despite a welcome victory over Barbarians in June, Lynn's side know they are still lacking in a number of areas, notably fitness.

It is a key focus for strength and conditioning coach Gareth Harris who is out on the main pitch encouraging the players through an intense set of interval runs.

Keira Bevan is rigged with a social media microphone as she races her opposite number to a marked cone.

"We need to work harder," Harris said.

"We know where we are from a physical perspective and it is about moving that dial forward. A lot of the girls are pretty sore, but that's okay, it's all in the plan."

The 46-strong extended squad has been in camp since 3 August and trained through soaring temperatures, but Harris - who linked up with Wales before last summer's Rugby World Cup - says the attitude has been "exceptional".

"You really see the girls going 'this is important for us'," Harris said.

"We want to be better. We want to be the best team we can be. We don't just want to turn up to the international stage, we want to dominate games.

"There's ownership of the work that they're doing and ownership of our standards and how we elevate those standards and accountability to each person.

"Everybody is going 'this is what I expect of you', which is perfect for us.

"I think we'll see a different Wales this time round."

Harris' optimism is echoed by forwards coach Steve Salvin who has come up to the vantage point of the barn balcony.

He clearly feels at home here having joined Lynn's backroom staff on a permanent basis with Ashley Beck in the summer.

"The four of us [coaches] were thrown together a little bit for the Six Nations, firefighting would be the wrong way to put it but obviously we were working in silos to get things sorted. Now we can be much more cohesive and collective around the way we go about doing things," Salvin said.

"We feel like there's growth in our set piece, our attack, our defence, we're essentially trying to cover all bases.

"During the Six Nations we performed reasonably well for probably 50 to 60 minutes, so one of the things we really need to go after for this series of games is performing for 80 minutes.

"If we do that, we'll give ourselves a much better chance of coming out the right side of the results."

Wales have only tasted success twice since Lynn took over in March 2025, the aforementioned Barbarians game and the first Test against Australia last summer.

But the autumn series will be seen as a major opportunity to get some wins on the board and climb back up the world rankings, where Wales were as high as sixth just three years ago.

And with the new-look WXV feeding into 2029 Rugby World Cup qualification - and a first ever Women's British and Irish Lions tour of New Zealand next September - there is plenty at stake for this group of pre-season players.

title: Ireland seal highest World Cup finish despite loss
description: Ireland will face either New Zealand or Pakistan ninth place at the World Cup despite Sunday's 2-1 defeat by France.
fullText:
Ireland will face either New Zealand or Pakistan ninth place at the World Cup following Sunday's 2-1 defeat by France.

Mark Tumilty’s side knew they were going to top the crossover Pool H before they took to the pitch in Wavre after South Africa and Malaysia had drawn 3-3.

Previous wins over both those countries meant Ireland could not be caught.

This perhaps helped to explain the performance against France who themselves were looking to avoid being in the classification game for last place.

It means Ireland will enter Friday's game assured of their their highest-ever finish, regardless of the result, having previously finished 12th in 1978 and 1990.

Both sides struggled to create any meaningful chances in the first half and it took until halfway through the third quarter before the first penalty corner was awarded.

It was Ireland who took the lead when Jeremy Duncan’s pressure turned the ball over and he then rounded the goalkeeper and slotted home the opening goal.

France continued to press hard and after being denied twice from a penalty corner, Victor Charlet fired his side level.

It was all France in the final quarter but just when it seemed Ireland were going to hold for a draw, Timottee Clement popped up to turn the ball past Jamie Carr from close range with just over a minute remaining to secure a place in the game for 13th place and vital world-ranking points.

“Just a disappointing result, to be honest,” said Ireland’s Sean Murray of the defeat.

“In the end, I think we knew we were through to the ninth-to-tenth playoff, but it's important for ranking points and going forward for next year.”

Ireland and France have been battling in the world rankings for the sixth-placed European side which would see them seeded and guaranteed a quarter-final place at next summer’s EuroHockey finals instead of playing in an elimination pool.

With the quarter-finalists most likely securing a place in the Olympic qualifiers, there is a lot to play for in terms of the finishing position at the World Cup.

As Ireland are guaranteed to finish above France, it should secure that sixth seed for the Euros but that will only be confirmed once the tournament is over.

“Of course we knew for the rest of the tournament where we sat already going into the game after the result beforehand," Murray added.

"We also knew it's really important for next year, for the Euros with the higher-ranked team getting an automatic quarter-final.

“But every game we want to go out and get the win. It's always disappointing when you go out and you don't get it in the end. Credit to France, they're a top side.”

title: ‘We are hitting a different chapter’: OpenAI leader warns of threat of ‘persistent’ AI cyber-attacks
description:

A senior leader at OpenAI has said people should prepare to defend against “ongoing, persistent” cyber-attacks from AIs, as cutting-edge artificial intelligence models gain advanced capabilities to plan and launch offensives.

fullText:
Chris Lehane tells Guardian of need to implement new safety standards as critics say AI firms acting ‘recklessly’

A senior leader at OpenAI has said people should prepare to defend against “ongoing, persistent” cyber-attacks from AIs, as cutting-edge artificial intelligence models gain advanced capabilities to plan and launch offensives.

The leading AI company this week announced a pause in development of its most advanced internal models amid rising safety fears, and Chris Lehane, its chief global affairs officer, said: “We are hitting a different chapter, a different moment within AI, in terms of what the capabilities of this technology can do.”

He spoke to the Guardian after cutting-edge AI agents-in-training unexpectedly broke out of a supposedly secure “sandbox” environment, accessed the internet, and hacked into another company, Hugging Face in late July. OpenAI also said it could not rule out another new model, Astra, having “critical cybersecurity capability”.

OpenAI announced on Tuesday it has paused training of some frontier AI models to implement new safeguards, and it is unclear when training will restart after new guardrails have been put in place.

Mia Glaese, who leads safety and alignment work, said: “We are very far from everything running back to normal.” Sam Altman, the CEO, said: “Getting AI safety right is more important than any company’s momentum.”

Lehane admitted people would not “feel great” about the threat of attacks, and described the risk as coming from open-source models – many of which are developed in China – which are only a few months behind frontier closed models built by companies such as OpenAI.

“People are going to be able to access these open-source models and be able to have ongoing, persistent attacks on you, and you’re going to need to have really superior models to fend them off and defend [yourself],” he said. “That’s not necessarily going to make the public feel great about things. It is just the reality of where we’re going.”

The threat of cyber-attacks crippling businesses, infrastructure and the general public has rapidly risen to the top of the list of urgent concerns about AI. This week, the UK government’s National Cyber Security Centre urged caution over the use of AI agents, warning their safety controls can be bypassed and that an AI agent “does not have common sense”. It advised organisations to limit their autonomy: “You should always be able to ‘pull the plug’ and halt autonomous AI agent activity immediately.”

Lehane renewed calls for the US government to legislate to create rules for frontier AI safety, and said the fact that the most cutting-edge and unreleased AI models appear to be improving cyber offence faster than defence, was “among the reasons why I think it’s absolutely imperative that this country passes a national law that creates mandatory required safety standards, and within that the pause element would be inherent and endemic to that process”.

“You would not be able to release or deploy models unless you’re proving and guaranteeing a level of safety before they get out into the public,” he suggested. “I think you have to have a national version here in the US and from there, you can create an international version, because I do think, ultimately, you’re going to need some type of an international structure here.”

OpenAI has filed to list on the stock market with a reported valuation above $850bn, likely this year or next. It has been locked in a race with rival Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot, to develop more and more capable AI models. Anthropic is also expected to debut on the US stock market within the coming year at a mammoth valuation.

In a sign the Donald Trump administration is shifting from its laissez-faire approach to AI regulation amid an intense race to stay ahead of China’s progress, the US president in June issued an executive order encouraging pre-deployment testing for frontier models and of open-weights models when they get closer to the cutting edge.

The system will be voluntary and the approach has been criticised for a lack of transparency, but observers think it could pave the way for tougher steps. Demis Hassabis, president of Google DeepMind, has proposed a new standards body modelled on the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority, an idea backed by Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic.

“The window where you could see legislation happening is potentially in the first part of next year, when a new Congress comes in,” Lehane said. “I think there’s a growing political consensus that transcends political parties.”

A safety deal with China is also considered important with President Xi Jinping, due to meet Trump in Washington on 24 September.

“Given how important this technology is, given how fast it is moving, given the capabilities, the sooner those conversations begin, the quicker we can actually roll up our sleeves and get into the hard and difficult work and see if we can figure something out,” Lehane said.

The Hugging Face incident, and similar recent cases admitted by other AI companies, have sparked increasing claims from safety experts that AI companies have behaved recklessly as they race to win the AI race and, in the case of OpenAI and Anthropic, prepare to list shares on the stock market.

Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI researcher who quit in 2024 and last year founded a non-profit organisation that has warned unchecked AI progress will result in a 10-30% probability of human extinction, said leaders of frontier laboratories have “painted the world into a corner”.

His organisation, the AI Futures Project, predicts AI super-intelligence could be achieved by 2030, but is calling for governments to prevent that from happening until a decade later to give AI scientists time to reckon with the risks of the advancing capabilities.

“The current AIs are dangerous in some sense, but they’re nothing compared to the AIs of next year and compared to the AIs of a year later,” he told the Guardian. His organisation wants US and international governments to delay progress to avoid an uncontrolled “intelligence explosion”, the worst results of which could be “AI-driven existential catastrophe” caused, for example, by AIs taking control of military assets or bioweapons.

Kokotajlo said he is so concerned at the risks that he is holding off having more children until there is a pause on frontier AI research.

David Krueger, an AI professor, safety campaigner and former founding director of the UK government’s AI Security Institute, said: “Nobody should be building more powerful AI systems, because we don’t know how to control them, align them, and look inside and see what they’re thinking well enough.”

He called AI companies’ attitude to safety “terrible” and “unconscionable”.

“They are being really reckless and increasingly taking their hands off the wheel,” he said. “We’ve just seen what happens when you do that.”

Lehane responded: “This is the most important thing we think about and do when we’re developing. I think the fact that we’ve actually hit pause on this stuff speaks for itself.”

title: 'Bad fight, bad scoring': Teofimo Lopez's win over Rolly Romero sparks backlash from boxing world
description: Teofimo Lopez's WBA title win over Rolly Romero on Saturday came with its fair share of critics and controversy.
fullText:
Teofimo Lopez officially joined the exclusive club of three-division boxing world champions on Saturday night in Las Vegas, though his WBA title win over Rolando "Rolly" Romero didn't come without its share of critics and controversy.

Lopez (23-2, 13 KOs) appeared to soundly outbox a sleepy Romero (17-3, 13 KOs) inside the T-Mobile Arena to capture the WBA welterweight title in a fight that never really got out of first gear. The tepid nature of the bout perhaps shouldn't have come as a surprise, considering the well-documented friendship the two fighters have shared for more than a decade, yet it was a baffling 114-114 scorecard from judge Glenn Feldman that drew just as much — if not more — condemnation as Lopez and Romero's performances Saturday.

In a fight that many observers viewed as a rout, which saw Lopez out-punch Romero 124-73 in total punches and 62-49 in power punches, Feldman improbably scored the bout a draw — meaning if judges Max DeLuca (115-113 Lopez) and Tim Cheatham (116-112 Lopez) had agreed, Romero would've controversially left Las Vegas with the WBA world title still wrapped around his waist.

Fortunately, yet another boxing judging crisis was averted this time. But Lopez's win still invited a healthy mix of aspersions and praise from his fellow fighters, ranging from former opponent George Kambosos Jr. panning the bout as a "glorified sparring session," to recent foe Shakur Stevenson giving both Lopez and Romero their due credit.
